title: AI and Legal Education (letter to colleagues from the Dean)
pub: The University of Texas at Austin School of Law
author: Robert M. Chesney

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: Chesney accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI competence and independent legal judgment must be developed together, then adds a concrete institutional strategy: integrated training across all three years, verification-focused competencies, shared tool access, enforceable AI-free assessments, and AI-enabled tutoring. He also reinforces the synthesis’s caution that these measures rest mainly on institutional experience and predictions rather than measured long-term learning outcomes.
qs: But these goals are not in a zero-sum relationship.
A sound law school AI strategy needs to address each of these challenges thoughtfully (and must be continually reassessed given the rapid pace of change).

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: Chesney accepts that AI access or fluency alone is insufficient and materially develops the proposition through Texas Law’s combined model of traditional judgment, structured AI training, protected assessments and supervised educational uses across all three years. His institutional account illustrates implementation, though it does not provide measured evidence of durable competence.
qs: And that’s a good thing, because the lawyers most likely to flourish in the years ahead are those who both are adept at making wise use of AI capabilities and possess the same expert judgment and perspective that have always been the hallmarks of the best lawyers.

Our model maps the various learning objectives onto an array of both for-credit courses (including, for example, 1L Legal Research and Writing and upper level Professional Responsibility courses) and a bespoke set of practical training sessions that are not for-credit courses but rather a key component of our existing Professional Pathways Program (in which all students participate).

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Chesney accepts the cluster’s core view that AI readiness must be combined with preserved human judgment, educational rigor and continual reassessment. He materially extends it by translating competence risk into a three-part law-school strategy covering AI skills, assessment integrity and cognitive de-skilling, while identifying bounded, complementary uses such as Socratic tutoring.
qs: And that’s a good thing, because the lawyers most likely to flourish in the years ahead are those who both are adept at making wise use of AI capabilities and possess the same expert judgment and perspective that have always been the hallmarks of the best lawyers.
A sound law school AI strategy needs to address each of these challenges thoughtfully (and must be continually reassessed given the rapid pace of change).

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Chesney accepts the need for selective, human-centred AI deployment and materially extends it into legal education. He proposes a school-wide operating model combining practical training, professional safeguards and adaptable instruction across all three years, while recognising that ubiquitous AI access creates context-specific assessment risks.
qs: Our model maps the various learning objectives onto an array of both for-credit courses (including, for example, 1L Legal Research and Writing and upper level Professional Responsibility courses) and a bespoke set of practical training sessions that are not for-credit courses but rather a key component of our existing Professional Pathways Program (in which all students participate).
Unfortunately, ubiquitous student access to AI capabilities has serious implications for the integrity of our assessments in certain contexts.

st.t: Law-school policy: Staged use bridges bans and adoption
st.an: Chesney directly supports the cluster’s core proposition that law schools should develop AI proficiency alongside, rather than at the expense of, traditional legal judgment. His letter does not materially extend the cluster’s staged instructional model because it offers a strategic objective, not detailed curricular sequencing or empirical evidence.
qs: But these goals are not in a zero-sum relationship.

And that’s a good thing, because the lawyers most likely to flourish in the years ahead are those who both are adept at making wise use of AI capabilities and possess the same expert judgment and perspective that have always been the hallmarks of the best lawyers.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: Chesney supports the cluster’s adaptation-oriented account: lawyers should combine AI proficiency with enduring legal judgment, and legal education should develop both rather than treat them as competing goals. The source does not, however, provide evidence about displacement or directly assess the heightened risk to junior training pipelines.

kp.k: AI skills and traditional legal judgment are complementary
kp.d: Chesney rejects a zero-sum relationship between traditional legal education and AI training. He predicts that lawyers combining wise AI use with expert judgment and perspective will flourish, and makes that combination the overarching objective of the law school’s education strategy. He also identifies expanded access to justice as a potential benefit of AI, rather than an established outcome.
qs: But these goals are not in a zero-sum relationship. It is possible to pursue them both with excellence.

the lawyers most likely to flourish in the years ahead are those who both are adept at making wise use of AI capabilities and possess the same expert judgment and perspective that have always been the hallmarks of the best lawyers.
not least of which is AI’s potential to expand access to justice

kp.k: Education strategy must address three distinct AI challenges
kp.d: The letter distinguishes teaching AI knowledge and skills, preserving assessment integrity despite ubiquitous AI access, and protecting educational rigor against possible cognitive de-skilling. Chesney presents the strategy as a current institutional approach requiring continual reassessment, not a settled or empirically validated solution.
qs: AI poses at least three distinct challenges in the education context:
A sound law school AI strategy needs to address each of these challenges thoughtfully (and must be continually reassessed given the rapid pace of change).
What follows below is a snapshot of our current approach.

kp.k: Practice adoption motivates training, despite economic and utility uncertainty
kp.d: Chesney asserts that AI’s role in legal practice grew tremendously over the preceding two years and will more likely than not expand further. He qualifies that forecast with possible slowing from passing through full token costs and debate over particular legal use cases. His stated basis for preparing students is years of conversations with alumni and employers, not a quantified adoption study.
qs: The role of AI tools in legal practice has grown tremendously over the past two years.
More likely than not, that role will continue to expand (though headwinds associated with increasing passthrough of the full cost of token consumption may slow things down).
years of conversations with our alumni and employers have made it clear to me that we owe it to our students to prepare them well for the AI-impacted future in which they will practice.

kp.k: Foundational AI literacy includes agents, verification, and costs
kp.d: The school’s general learning objectives encompass model basics, choosing models and access routes, creating portable context layers, connecting tools and data sources, creating agents, checking outputs, and understanding service costs. These are intended learning objectives rather than reported student competencies or measured educational results.
qs: Understanding the significance of context layers and how to make them (including portability).
Understanding the utility of agents and how to create them.
Understanding the signal importance of output verification.
Understanding the cost structure of AI-related services.

kp.k: Legal AI competence requires verified work and defensible choices
kp.d: Practice-specific objectives include demonstrated production of verified work product, understanding legal-use risks, and comparing platform capabilities and economics. Students should justify tool choices in light of capabilities, risks, limitations, and costs, while understanding implications for professional ethics, privilege, work-product protection, court rules, and privacy or cybersecurity.
qs: Understanding leading use cases and having a demonstrable capacity to produce verified work product in one or more such contexts.
Understanding the comparative capabilities and economics of particular platforms.
Having the ability to make (and to articulate) justifiable selections among options for using AI in specific scenarios, accounting for capabilities, risks, limitations, and costs.

kp.k: Institutional licensing aims to equalize student AI access
kp.d: Chesney reports that students already received access to Harvey and Legora, with additional application-layer licenses forthcoming alongside Westlaw and Lexis offerings. He expects enterprise-grade frontier-lab licenses for all students, faculty, and staff in fall 2026. The equity rationale is that students differ in their ability or willingness to purchase premium access; the letter does not claim that equal educational outcomes have been demonstrated.
qs: We were in the first wave of law schools whose students received access to Harvey and Legora (leading AI application-layer platforms focused on legal practice), and there are more such application-layer licenses on the way (in addition to the offerings from incumbents Westlaw and Lexis).
Equally important, we also expect to have all our students (as well as all faculty and staff) on enterprise-grade licenses with leading frontier labs this fall.
Some but not all students can and will spend to have access to a premium tier.

kp.k: AI training spans coursework and practical professional development
kp.d: The school has developed a program mapping learning objectives onto credit-bearing courses, including 1L Legal Research and Writing and upper-level Professional Responsibility, plus noncredit practical sessions within the Professional Pathways Program, in which all students participate. Chesney argues that this structure enables adaptability, scheduling flexibility, and engagement throughout all three years.
qs: a bespoke set of practical training sessions that are not for-credit courses but rather a key component of our existing Professional Pathways Program (in which all students participate).
In this way, we achieve subject-matter adaptability, schedule flexibility, and the ability to keep students engaged with AI skills training across all three years of the law school experience.

kp.k: Unsupervised assessments threaten confidence in no-AI rules
kp.d: Where instructors prohibit AI, Chesney identifies take-home work and in-class assessments with unrestricted device functionality as vulnerable to unauthorized assistance. He distinguishes actual rule-breaking from the damaging perception that others are breaking rules. Where instructors intentionally allow AI, he says this particular concern largely recedes and assessments can instead examine thoughtful AI use.
qs: if a professor actually wants students to employ AI in some fashion in relation to an assignment, paper, or exam, this concern largely drops out.
This is particularly true for the take-home exam format, though really any assessment that allows students to work in an unsupervised setting has this same vulnerability.
Such settings also are vulnerable, notably, to the harmful perception that some are breaking the no-AI-use rule (even if no one actually is).

kp.k: Exam formats shifted toward controlled and live assessment
kp.d: Following faculty discussions before the previous academic year, Chesney reports near-complete elimination of take-home exams and a sharp increase in in-class exams using software that restricts device functions. He also reports increased interest in participation, presentations, and sometimes oral exams. These are institutional observations without numerical counts or measured effects on misconduct.
qs: The end result was the near-complete elimination of take-home exams, and a sharp increase in in-class exams requiring use of software limiting what can be done on the device (thus precluding resort to AI).
By the same token, we’ve also seen a surge of interest in assessments involving class participation and live presentations (even oral exams in some cases).

kp.k: Writing seminars remain an unresolved assessment-integrity challenge
kp.d: Extended, largely independent research and writing projects remain difficult to protect against prohibited AI assistance. Some faculty now require documentation of AI use at specified writing stages and evaluate its quality, aligning assessment with emerging skills. Chesney treats this as an option for willing instructors, not a universal answer, and calls for further solutions where AI remains prohibited.
qs: Alas, a significant assessment-integrity challenge remains: our writing seminars (and any other course that calls for students to produce an academic paper through work performed outside of class hours).

they have amended their rules to include affirmative requirements for students to document their use of AI at specific steps in the writing process, and are evaluating them at least in part on the quality of that AI use.
For others who prefer to keep AI at bay in this setting, however, more creativity will be needed.

kp.k: AI tutoring could complement, not replace, faculty interaction
kp.d: Chesney identifies practice-exam generation and patient, discreet, always-available tutoring as beneficial educational uses. He emphasizes access to relevant course materials and instructions to teach Socratically rather than supply answers. He predicts tutoring will complement office hours while preserving faculty interactions’ distinctive mentoring value and certainty about the professor’s understanding.
qs: It can be used to generate practice exams, for example, including ones informed by the specific professor’s back catalogue of exam questions (if those are made available).

AI also has tremendous potential to serve as an always-available, patient, and discreet tutor, especially if the model has access to the relevant course materials and is instructed to play the tutorial role in a Socratic manner rather than just giving answers.
the custom- tutoring use case for AI is likely to emerge as a powerful complement to office hours

kp.k: AI shortcuts risk undermining independent legal skill formation
kp.d: Chesney argues that outsourcing learning tasks may substitute superficial answers for the difficult work needed to develop analysis, doctrinal perspective, discernment, communication, and judgment. The risk extends beyond graded work to reading and synthesizing assigned materials. He predicts AI will tempt students more than older shortcuts because of availability, confidentiality, range, and iterative dialogue, while acknowledging that many students will resist. The letter offers a risk argument, not measured evidence of de-skilling.
qs: AI also can be used as shortcut that quickly and easily puts an answer into a student’s hands, replacing deeper learning with a more-superficial semblance.
This is so due to AI’s comparative availability, confidentiality, and range, as well as its distinct capacity for iterative dialogue.
These qualities will tempt more students more often to spend less time wrestling directly with the assigned materials (or even to skip such direct engagement outright).
there are plenty of students who resist this temptation and will continue to do so, understanding that de-skilling is a serious and harmful risk.

kp.k: Supervised Socratic dialogue becomes more educationally valuable
kp.d: Because AI use cannot reliably be excluded outside supervised settings, Chesney recommends sustained, rigorous classroom dialogue that makes students analyze and communicate independently. Lecturing or brief, light questioning will not fully realize this opportunity; faculty should also prevent screen distraction or reliance during dialogue. He frames renewed Socratic teaching and exhortations to do independent work as partial mitigation, not a complete solution.
qs: It’s not a silver bullet, but I believe it will help to a degree.
supervised settings have become even more valuable than they used to be.
faculty need to make extensive use of classroom time to engage students in sustained and rigorous dialogue.
This points towards a renewed emphasis on the Socratic mode of teaching.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Chesney predicts continued expansion of AI in legal practice and argues that successful lawyers will combine AI proficiency with traditional legal expertise.
pts.d: Robert M. Chesney states that AI's role in practice has grown substantially and is more likely than not to expand further, although passing through the full costs of token consumption could slow adoption. He predicts that lawyers best positioned to flourish will use AI wisely while retaining analytical capacity, legal perspective, communication skills and expert judgment. This is an augmentation-oriented account rather than a prediction that AI will replace lawyers. He also identifies expanded access to justice as a potential benefit, without specifying a mechanism or scale.

pts.k: Chesney argues that legal education can preserve traditional rigor while integrating sustained, practical AI training and more equitable tool access.
pts.d: He rejects a zero-sum relationship between traditional pedagogy and AI skills. UT's described response combines for-credit courses with practical training throughout the three-year degree. Learning objectives include selecting tools with attention to capabilities, risks and costs; creating agents; verifying output; producing verified legal work product; and understanding professional ethics, privilege, court rules and security implications. School-provided premium access is intended to reduce differences arising from students' ability or willingness to pay. These are stated educational objectives and institutional arrangements, not demonstrated learning outcomes.

pts.k: Ubiquitous AI access makes unsupervised assessments vulnerable and has already prompted changes to UT's assessment practices.
pts.d: Chesney identifies take-home exams, out-of-class papers and in-class assessments with unrestricted device access as vulnerable when AI use is prohibited. He distinguishes actual rule-breaking from perceptions of unfairness, which can also undermine confidence. He reports near-elimination of take-home exams, increased use of device-restricting exam software, and increased interest in participation, live presentations and oral exams. Writing seminars remain an unresolved challenge. Some faculty instead require documented AI use and evaluate its quality, aligning assessment with new professional skills.

pts.k: AI can support learning through practice exams and tailored tutoring, but may also encourage shortcuts that weaken students' development of core legal capabilities.
pts.d: Chesney predicts that AI tutoring will become a powerful complement to office hours, particularly when grounded in course materials and configured to ask Socratic questions rather than supply answers. Conversely, he predicts that AI's availability, confidentiality, breadth and iterative dialogue will make it more tempting than previous shortcuts, leading more students to engage less directly with difficult readings and assignments. He presents cognitive de-skilling as a risk, not a measured outcome, and acknowledges that many students will resist shortcuts.

pts.k: Chesney argues that AI increases the educational value of supervised classroom work and renewed Socratic teaching.
pts.d: Because reliably preventing AI use outside supervision is not possible in his account, Chesney regards classroom time as increasingly important for ensuring students independently analyze and communicate difficult ideas. He recommends sustained, rigorous dialogue involving all students and attention to device distraction or reliance. He does not claim that supervision alone or passive lectures solve the problem; he presents this approach as a partial mitigation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on Chesney's institutional experience, alumni and employer conversations, reported faculty practices and pedagogical reasoning, rather than quantitative studies.
pts.d: His rationale for preparing students for AI-influenced practice draws explicitly on years of conversations with alumni and employers. His assessment claims include first-person institutional reporting about faculty deliberations and subsequent exam changes. He also reports tool access and curricular arrangements as concrete institutional actions, including access to Harvey and Legora, which are legal-AI platforms rather than legal service providers. Predictions about future professional success, tutoring, shortcutting and the benefits of Socratic teaching are reasoned judgments. The letter supplies no adoption dataset, model benchmark, measured cheating or de-skilling rate, controlled educational evaluation, or evidence quantifying access-to-justice benefits.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The June 16, 2026 letter combines retrospective institutional observations with near-term educational plans and open-ended predictions.
pts.d: The reported growth of AI in practice covers the preceding two years, approximately mid-2024 to mid-2026. Assessment changes followed faculty discussions before the last academic year. Enterprise-grade frontier-model licenses are expected in fall 2026, and requests to instructors concern the coming academic year. Predictions about professional success and tutoring extend into unspecified future years. Expansion in practice is qualified by cost pressures and disagreement over utility in particular use cases. Assessment-integrity concerns primarily apply where AI is disallowed; de-skilling concerns apply where students substitute AI for independent work. Tutoring benefits depend especially on relevant materials and Socratic configuration, while classroom mitigation depends on active dialogue rather than lecturing. Chesney emphasizes that the strategy and learning objectives must evolve.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are law students, faculty, law schools, employers and future lawyers; clients and the public are addressed more indirectly.
pts.d: Students face new AI competency expectations, unequal paid-tool access, altered assessments, opportunities for tutoring and risks to independent skill development. Faculty must reconsider assessment integrity and teaching methods; writing-seminar instructors receive particular attention. Law schools must combine AI upskilling with traditional professional formation. Employers depend on credible assessment measures and graduates prepared for AI-influenced practice. Future lawyers are expected to need both wise AI use and established professional judgment, including judgment in client communications. Faculty and staff are also intended recipients of enterprise licenses. People with unmet legal needs are potential beneficiaries of the stated access-to-justice opportunity, but the source does not identify specific populations or quantify effects. It makes no segment-specific predictions about law-firm staffing, ALSP competition, billing models or employment displacement.
